<reason>B seized the decisive frame early and never lost it: caps are a rationing device, so the real question is "which 5,000?", and any rule is a distribution rule. A's opening largely attacked a purpose B never claimed (footfall reduction), and although A adapted well by proposing neutral rationing (lottery, long booking windows), B's "rounding error" pressure question forced A into an answer — residents can try "in March, in November, on a rainy Tuesday" — that concedes the peak-season access the motion is specifically about. B's closing crystallized that with precision. B also answered A's sharpest pressure question directly and plausibly (existing municipal register covering resident/worker/student, tax-liability fraud resistance, and the asymmetry that over-inclusion costs B little while A needs a perfect line); A's second rebuttal simply asserted the line problem was "never closed" without engaging the register answer, which is an execution cost. On revenue, A built a real dilemma (either the discount costs conservation euros or repricing makes the carve-out unnecessary), but B answered honestly that access, not revenue, is the objective and that "do both" keeps the fund whole under a binding cap — so A's closing framing of the motion as "a tax on the fragile thing" no longer tracked, since both sides' caps protect the plaster. A's best surviving point (residents' many low-cost attempts versus a tourist's one) was genuine but undercut by A's own off-peak phrasing. B also left the consent/political-economy argument essentially unanswered.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's closing exploitation of A's own answer: A defended neutral rationing by saying residents can enter in "March, in November, on a rainy Tuesday," and B showed that this concedes exactly the peak-season exclusion the motion targets — "the whole dispute is peak season." Paired with B's direct register-based answer to A's fraud/line-drawing question, this neutralized A's strongest live route.</best_rebuttal>
